dialogue.text: [serious, engaging] And this is where it reaches you. America's biggest tech companies own millions of those same chips, and those few companies make up more than a third of the S&P 500, the list of big companies most Americans' retirement money is bet on. Say your job puts part of every paycheck into a retirement fund, and it's grown to ten thousand dollars. You open the app at lunch and it says nine thousand one hundred. By Friday, eight thousand.
[quiet, serious] Remember that number. In a few weeks, you'll be tempted to do the one thing that turns a bad month into a lost decade, and almost everybody does it.
[serious, engaging] Day two, and the crash takes a detour through Tokyo that ends at your car loan.

[serious, engaging] For years, big investors borrowed money in Japan, where loans cost almost nothing, and used it to buy American stocks. Now those stocks are falling, the loans still have to be paid back, and everyone runs for the same exit at once.
I'm selling everything to pay back the loan. So is everyone else on this floor. So who's buying?
[serious, engaging] Nobody. On August 5th, 2024, a small version of this trade came apart, and Japan's stock market fell twelve percent in a single day.

[serious, engaging] Here's how it comes back to you. Japan owns more American government IOUs than any other country, and when Japanese investors need cash, they sell them. When lots get sold at once, America has to pay higher interest to keep borrowing, and that spreads to every loan. Japan sold about thirty billion dollars of them in just the first three months of this year, and American rates went up. In our crash, it's many times that, so your mortgage, your car loan and your credit card get more expensive the same week your savings shrank.
